doc.title: Joseph Daley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 18, 2018

chapter: Howard Johnson and the loft scene
title: Howard Johnson and Herb Bushler in the Gil Evans orchestra
summary: Johnson interacts with bassist Herb Bushler, as on Bengali and Thoroughbred, and passes the approach to later tubists.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: How did that work with — the working with the bassist?

Oh yeah that’s the whole thing. In that band it was a bass player, his name was Herb Bushler. And him and Howard were like very good friends. And what Howard would do is he would listen to what Herb was playing on the bass, and he would pull out certain parts of what Herb was playing and incorporate those into the tuba part. So Howard was not only playing tuba parts, sectional parts, he was also playing tuba bass parts in conjunction with the bass player. And then at certain points he would say okay well rather than play with him, let’s say if Herb is going up maybe if I go contrary down and go down and do that. So you know he would definitely work — that’s the trick of the trade. You just can’t play anything. You have to be listening to the people around you, what they do. And him and Herb became like a thing, where I mean if you listen to that album “Bengali” you listen to that and just listen to Howard Johnson and Herb Bushler on a piece called “Thoroughbred” written by Billy Harper. And just listen to how they interact and you see exactly what I mean with that. That’s a prime example. I saw, because I was in the band at that time. In fact I’m on that record. I saw how Howard evolved with Herb from the time the arrangement came in until the time the arrangement was recorded. So you saw that evolution. And then Howard, you know, singlehandedly evolved the tuba, because then he passed it on to people like Bob Stewart, Dave Bargeron, Earl McIntyre, and a host of other people he passed this information on. And everybody that plays tuba now does that. Now it’s just like expected of a tuba player and be able to play whatever’s written and then listen to the bass player and when he has like open space you know, join the bass player and play in conjunction with the bass player and then if we have enough time to evolve to the point where you begin to do counter- lines against him, against what the bass is doing.
